🇯🇵 Japan’s rearmament dreams crash into supply roadblocks
Tokyo is pushing ahead with plans to beef up its armed forces and sharpen its strike capabilities, an expansion that's raised eyebrows across the region over just how far its military ambitions will go. Yet the buildup faces serious obstacles, the SCMP reports:
🔶 Japan has 118 outstanding orders for US military equipment to the tune of about $7.2 billion, some delayed by five years or more.
🔶 Deliveries of up to 400 Tomahawk missiles could be pushed back as far as two years while the US replenishes its depleted stocks
🔶 Spare-parts shortages have reportedly left only about 12 of Japan's roughly 40 Kawasaki P-1 patrol aircraft mission-ready
🔶 F-35 deliveries are also behind schedule, with 34 of the 42 ordered jets still outstanding as of late March
Even with these challenges, Tokyo is reworking its defense strategy — pursuing expanded counterstrike capabilities and closer military-industrial ties with Washington. This effort marks another step away from Japan's traditionally defensive posture.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇨🇳 China trains infantry to fight and survive in drone-dominated battlefield
China's infantry units are reworking their training, equipment, and tactics around the threat from drones after exercises exposed how vulnerable traditional camouflage has become, the South China Morning Post reports.
The army responded by writing new instructional manuals, building dedicated counter-drone training facilities including simulation rooms, and shifting the focus of exercises toward detecting and disrupting hostile drones with specialized weapons and coordinated infantry responses. Officers are now required to demonstrate proficiency with counter-drone equipment and tactics, not just conventional infantry skills.
The shift is visible across much of the force:
🌏 A 71st Group Army brigade ordered compulsory training on concealing heat sources and lights at night, including covering the hot parts of rocket launchers
🌏 A 72nd Group Army amphibious armored company worked with multiple manufacturers to improve its use of uncrewed systems and counter-drone equipment
🌏 Troops from the 78th Group Army trained to evade reconnaissance drones
🌏 81st Group Army reconnaissance units used insulating blankets, damp soil, and turf to reduce the heat signatures that give away their positions
Chinese manufacturers have produced handheld and vehicle-mounted counter-drone systems and detection equipment, while individual formations experiment with their own solutions, including protective cages fitted to armored vehicles.
Recent conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have highlighted the dominance of drones across battlefields, raising the need to adapt troops to the new rules of modern warfare.

events.text:
🇪🇺🛢📉 How Europeans Will Pay for US-Israel War on Iran
Europe is approaching winter with depleted gas reserves and prices near three times their February level, leaving households and factories exposed if temperatures plunge. The US-Israeli war against Iran has disrupted supplies just as the continent needs enough fuel to cover its peak heating demand.
The European gas benchmark crossed €100 per megawatt-hour on October 28 for the first time since 2022. EU storage was only 75% full on October 21, according to EU energy regulator ACER, leaving a much thinner cushion against cold weather and interruptions to imports.
Europe’s growing reliance on liquefied natural gas, cooled for transport by ship, makes a cold spell in Asia a European problem too. Buyers compete for available cargoes, so higher Asian demand can push up the price Europe must pay even when its own weather stays mild.
ACER says no significant volumes of Qatari liquefied gas reached the EU over the summer. US supplies now account for roughly 30% of the bloc’s total gas supply, as Qatari and Russian deliveries have fallen. Reducing dependence on Russia has left Europe more exposed to American exports and competition in global shipping markets.
The cost reaches well beyond heating bills. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has added €127B to Europe’s fossil fuel import bill without buying any additional energy. Governments already carrying heavy debts face pressure to subsidize consumers while businesses absorb higher operating costs.
Bloomberg describes a 182-year-old German porcelain factory preparing to shut its kilns and Polish fertilizer producers seeking government intervention. For industries that need large amounts of heat or gas, prolonged high prices can turn a temporary production cut into a permanent closure.
Forecasts of a broadly mild winter offer some relief, but an average seasonal temperature cannot rule out damaging cold spells. A burst of heating demand would drain storage faster; simultaneous cold in Asia would make replacement cargoes more expensive.
Europe is paying for a war launched by its own allies. Subsidies can spread the bill, but they cannot replace missing gas. A severe winter would force European governments to spend more protecting households from the fallout while manufacturers face deeper cuts, closures and lost competitiveness.
